items.prompt: What is a "flaky test"?
choices: A test that produces different results (pass or fail) across runs of the same code with no relevant input change
A test that always fails, regardless of the code
A test that takes longer than 5 seconds to run
A test written without any assertions
items.explanation: Flakiness is specifically about inconsistent outcomes on unchanged code — not about slowness, structure, or always failing.

items.prompt: In the Scenario, is the failing test itself likely to have a wrong assertion?
choices: Not necessarily — flakiness is almost never about the assertion being wrong; it's about the outcome secretly depending on something outside the test's control
Yes — a flaky test always has an incorrect assertion that needs rewriting
Yes, because flaky tests are defined as tests with syntax errors
No — flaky tests are always caused by a bug in the test framework itself
items.explanation: The logic under test is usually fine — flakiness comes from an uncontrolled dependency like shared state, real timing, or unawaited async work, not a wrong assertion.

items.prompt: What is "non-determinism" as this unit uses the term?
choices: A test's outcome can vary between runs of identical code, because it depends on something that isn't fixed
A test that produces a compiler warning
A test that runs in a different programming language than the code it tests
A test that has more than one assertion
items.explanation: Non-determinism is about the outcome varying run to run on the same code — driven by things like the system clock, randomness, or scheduling that aren't fixed.

items.prompt: Which of these introduces non-determinism into a test?
choices: Using the real system clock (`Date.now()`) instead of a fixed, injected time
Using a descriptive test name
Splitting a large test file into two smaller files
Adding a comment explaining what the test checks
items.explanation: The real system clock varies between runs and machines — relying on it directly (rather than a fixed/injected time) is a classic source of non-determinism.

items.prompt: What does "test isolation" mean?
choices: One test's outcome doesn't depend on whether, or in what order, any other test ran before it
Each test must run in its own separate process
Tests must be physically located in separate files
A test can only call one function from the code under test
items.explanation: Isolation is about independence between test outcomes, not about physical separation of files or processes (though those can help achieve it).

items.prompt: In the Scenario, do the two tests sharing `orderStore` have test isolation?
choices: No — one test's writes to the shared store affect what the other test reads, so their outcomes depend on execution order
Yes — since they're in the same file, they're automatically isolated from each other
Yes, as long as they don't call the same function
It depends only on whether the tests are named alphabetically in run order
items.explanation: Sharing a mutable store without resetting it is exactly what breaks isolation — one test's outcome becomes dependent on whatever the other test left behind.

items.prompt: What is "environment leakage"?
choices: State created or modified by one test that isn't cleaned up, and ends up affecting a different test that runs afterward
A test that reads an environment variable
A memory leak in the production code being tested
A test suite that takes too long to run in a CI environment
items.explanation: Environment leakage is specifically about leftover state crossing from one test into another — not about environment variables or memory leaks in general.

items.prompt: In the Scenario's bug, what leaked from one test into another?
choices: An order left in the module-level `orderStore` array by one test, which the next test's `getPendingOrders()` call then saw
A network connection that stayed open between tests
An environment variable set by the CI runner
A file left on disk after the test suite finished
items.explanation: The leaked state was the leftover order in the shared in-memory array — nothing on disk, no environment variable, no network connection involved.

items.prompt: The Scenario's test suite passes 100/100 times locally but fails about 1 in 20 times in CI, with no code changes in between. What does this most likely indicate?
choices: The test's outcome depends on something (like execution order) that stays constant locally but varies in CI
CI machines are simply less reliable hardware than developer laptops
The test framework has a bug that only manifests in CI environments
The code under test has a genuine, code-level bug that only affects 5% of runs
items.explanation: A consistent local order hides an order-dependency that CI's different execution conditions (shuffled order, parallelism) can expose — the code itself isn't the problem.

items.prompt: Why does re-running the exact same failing CI commit often make the test pass again?
choices: Because the underlying dependency (like execution order or timing) that triggered the failure is itself non-deterministic, so a different run may not hit the same triggering condition
Because CI automatically fixes flaky tests on a second attempt
Because the code silently changes between CI runs
Because re-running always uses a completely different, more reliable server
items.explanation: Since the failure depends on a condition (order, timing) that varies between runs, a re-run may simply not reproduce the specific condition that caused the earlier failure.

items.prompt: Per L2's table, which of these is a source of flakiness from "real randomness"?
choices: A test relies on `Math.random()` or a real UUID generator without a fixed seed
A test uses two variables with very similar names
A test imports a module that isn't used
A test file is longer than 200 lines
items.explanation: Unseeded randomness produces a different value every run, making any assertion tied to a specific value unreliable — that's the "real randomness" category.

items.prompt: Does L2 present these four causes of flakiness as unfixable, inherent risks of testing async or stateful code?
choices: No — every one of the four causes has a deterministic fix (reset state, inject a fake clock, seed randomness, actually await async work)
Yes — flaky tests involving async code can never be made fully reliable
Yes, but only shared-state leakage is fixable; the other three are inherent
No — but only if the test suite is rewritten in a different language
items.explanation: L2 explicitly states each cause has a deterministic fix — flakiness is a sign of an uncontrolled dependency, not an unavoidable property of testing async or stateful code.

items.prompt: Per L2's flowchart, why does a shared-state bug often stay invisible on a single developer's local machine?
choices: Local runs tend to execute tests in the same fixed order every time, so if that order never triggers the dependency, the bug never surfaces
Local machines automatically reset all shared state between every test
Local test runners are incapable of running more than one test
Local runs always use a completely different codebase than CI
items.explanation: A consistently fixed local execution order means only one of the possible orderings ever actually runs — if that one happens not to expose the dependency, it stays hidden.

items.prompt: Why does CI trigger order-dependent bugs more often than local runs, per L2?
choices: CI frequently shuffles test order and runs tests across multiple parallel workers, increasing the chance of hitting the triggering order
CI runs each test exactly once and never repeats a test suite
CI machines have faster processors, which somehow causes more bugs
CI always runs tests in strict alphabetical order, unlike local machines
items.explanation: Shuffled or parallelized execution increases the odds of hitting whatever ordering actually triggers an order-dependency, compared to a single developer's fixed local order.

items.prompt: Does L2 argue that CI itself is "flakier" or somehow the source of the problem?
choices: No — CI isn't introducing new bugs, it's exposing bugs that were always there but never had the right conditions to surface locally
Yes — CI environments are inherently unreliable compared to local machines
Yes, but only for tests written in JavaScript
No — but only because CI machines are physically closer to the production servers
items.explanation: L2 explicitly rejects the framing of CI as inherently flakier — the bug pre-exists in the code, CI just has a wider range of execution conditions that can trigger it.

items.prompt: Per L2, is "it passes locally" strong proof that a test suite has no flakiness issues?
choices: No — local runs are a much narrower sample of possible execution conditions than CI actually exercises
Yes — if a test suite passes locally every time, it's guaranteed to be deterministic
Yes, as long as it's run at least three times locally
No, but only for test suites larger than 100 tests
items.explanation: Passing consistently under one narrow set of local conditions doesn't rule out a dependency that only certain orderings or timings (more common in CI) would expose.

items.prompt: Per L2's failure modes, what's wrong with re-running a failing test until it passes and moving on?
choices: It treats the symptom, not the cause — the underlying non-determinism is still there and will trigger again
It's fine, since a passing re-run proves the code is correct
It's wrong only because it wastes CI compute time, not because of any correctness issue
It's the recommended standard practice for handling all test failures
items.explanation: Re-running until green doesn't fix the underlying uncontrolled dependency — the same flakiness will resurface on a future run.

items.prompt: Per L2, why is adding a longer `setTimeout` delay a weak fix for a race-condition flaky test?
choices: It narrows the window for the race without eliminating it — still non-deterministic, and now harder to reproduce and debug when it does fail
It's actually a complete fix, since a long enough delay always eliminates race conditions
It's wrong only because longer delays are against most style guides
It has no effect on race conditions either way
items.explanation: A longer delay reduces how often the race is lost, but doesn't remove the race itself — the test remains non-deterministic, just less likely to fail on any given run.

items.prompt: Fix makeOrderStore/addOrderTo/getPendingOrdersFrom so that a freshly-made store never sees state left behind by a previously-made store — no test's writes should be visible to a different store.

tests.description: adding to one store doesn't affect a different store made afterward
tests.expr: expect((() => { const s1 = makeOrderStore(); addOrderTo(s1, { status: "pending" }); const s2 = makeOrderStore(); return getPendingOrdersFrom(s2).length; })()).toBe(0)

tests.description: a store correctly reflects its own added order
tests.expr: expect((() => { const s = makeOrderStore(); addOrderTo(s, { status: "pending" }); return getPendingOrdersFrom(s).length; })()).toBe(1)

items.explanation: Returning a brand-new array from makeOrderStore, instead of a shared module-level one, means every call gets its own independent store — nothing written to one store is ever visible from another, which is exactly what removes the order-dependency.
items.reference:
❌ Shared store — one array, reused across every test
✅ Fresh store per test — makeStore() returns a new array every call

Why: a test can only be order-independent if it never shares mutable state with another test.

items.prompt: Fix makeLogStore/addLogTo/getErrorLogsFrom so that a freshly-made store never sees state left behind by a previously-made store — no test's writes should be visible to a different store.

tests.description: adding to one store doesn't affect a different store made afterward
tests.expr: expect((() => { const s1 = makeLogStore(); addLogTo(s1, { level: "error" }); const s2 = makeLogStore(); return getErrorLogsFrom(s2).length; })()).toBe(0)

tests.description: a store correctly reflects only its own error-level entries
tests.expr: expect((() => { const s = makeLogStore(); addLogTo(s, { level: "error" }); addLogTo(s, { level: "info" }); return getErrorLogsFrom(s).length; })()).toBe(1)

items.explanation: Same fix as any shared-state leak: return a new array per call instead of reusing one module-level array, so two separately-made stores can never see each other's entries.
items.reference:
❌ Shared store — one array, reused across every test
✅ Fresh store per test — makeStore() returns a new array every call

Why: a test can only be order-independent if it never shares mutable state with another test.

items.prompt: Fix isOrderExpired so it takes the current time as a parameter instead of reading the real system clock internally.

tests.description: an order past its TTL is expired, given a fixed now
an order within its TTL is not expired, given a fixed now
the same order and now always give the same result

items.explanation: Accepting `now` as a parameter instead of reading `Date.now()` internally makes the function's output depend only on its arguments — a test can pass any fixed `now` value and get a deterministic, repeatable result instead of one tied to whatever moment the test happened to run.
items.reference:
❌ Reads the real clock — Date.now() gives a different value every run
✅ Takes now as a parameter — the caller (or the test) controls exactly what time it is

Why: a function that depends on the real clock can never be tested deterministically — injecting the time turns it back into a pure function.

items.prompt: Fix isSessionExpired so it takes the current time as a parameter instead of reading the real system clock internally.

tests.description: a session past its timeout is expired, given a fixed now
a session within its timeout is not expired, given a fixed now
the same session and now always give the same result

items.explanation: Same fix as any real-time dependency: take `now` as a parameter instead of reading the system clock inside the function, so the result depends only on the arguments and is fully reproducible in a test.
items.reference:
❌ Reads the real clock — Date.now() gives a different value every run
✅ Takes now as a parameter — the caller (or the test) controls exactly what time it is

Why: a function that depends on the real clock can never be tested deterministically — injecting the time turns it back into a pure function.
